summary:
Cusco stands under the national framework of Peru, where trans identity is not criminalised but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. No department-level trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding could be located for Cusco; all sources attached to this jurisdiction are national in scope, and every binding rule below applies in Cusco as elsewhere in Peru.

In February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously, for plenary debate, a merged draft opinion of bills 6506 and 8457 introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their sex at birth. The exceptions listed cover custody situations, cases requiring medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the package also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The legislative trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport in Lima.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for the narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same determination for restrooms generally, reaching trans youth, and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement reaches private and public life and rests on individual judgement rather than official verification. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access would depend on security staff's personal assessment, including checks of identity documents, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and, by the account of those who compile it, under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, released in July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of which 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denunciations in 2020. Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The figures are national and cover Cusco as part of Peru; no regional deviation is documented either way.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom provision stands in direct conflict with external protection machinery. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The legal analysis of Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte at IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, argues that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The February 2025 commission debate sits within a wider pattern of official hostility. Speech and association are constrained by vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content that enables censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Recorded attacks show the form violence takes. The Observatorio report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cusco live under the same national restrictions as visitors, without an exemption for habitual presence. Restroom entry is determined by 'biological sex' under the April 2025 law, so a trans resident faces the security-staff and identity-document assessment described above in shopping centres, gyms, cinemas, health facilities and municipal buildings, as well as in workplaces. The consumer-protection body's dismissal of a complaint against a gym that applied the policy indicates that administrative channels offer little recourse for these disputes.

Inclusive signage is banned, which removes 'women in their diversity' and comparable wording from shops, public bodies, schools and event materials. The vague child-protection articles of the same law, including the article 4 ban on media and advertising content, expose residents who produce artistic, educational or identity-related material to censorship, and the obscenity minimum sentence rose from three to four years.

Two protective developments are on record for residents. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Because LGBT provisions were removed from the Penal Code in 2017, a resident who is assaulted because of their gender identity has no hate-crime coverage under that statute; the Azul Rojas Marín judgment came through the Inter-American system after decades of litigation rather than through ordinary domestic hate-crime prosecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the April 2025 bathroom provision and the inclusive-signage ban are being applied by municipal authorities, private security firms or health facilities in Cusco is unresolved: the three sources attached to this jurisdiction are national in scope, and none documents an enforcement incident, fine, ejection or complaint inside the department.

No Cusco-specific data on killings, denunciations or police conduct toward trans people is sourced here. The 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases for 2020-2023 are national totals, and their distribution across departments is not stated; the possibility of a higher or lower rate in Cusco than the national figure is not sourced either way.

The claim that enforcement depends on security staff checking identity documents rests on an activist's warning recorded in February 2025, not on a documented practice in Cusco. No rule governing the gender marker on Peruvian identity or travel documents is stated in the inventory, so document-screening practice at entry and in local identification checks remains unresolved.

The current implementation status and any constitutional challenge to the April 2025 law itself, as distinct from the July 2025 ruling against an anti-equality decree in Lima, are not sourced.
